title: Harry Kane Has the Big Learning Message
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Martin Skelton uses Harry Kane’s acceptance speech for the 2026 Ballon d’Or, in which Kane said it is always about getting better, as a definition of learning. Kane was long considered merely good, and his rise came through steady improvement, which Skelton calls his Hedgehog Concept. For Skelton, learning means getting better and making that improvement sticky, which he links to the idea of good struggle followed by consolidation. He argues that getting better means knowing more than before, performing a skill better than before and deepening understanding, without needing to be perfect or the best. He calls on teachers to design experiences of good struggle that are hard enough to require effort but not so hard that students learn they cannot. He closes by urging schools to celebrate improvement rather than the best, because focusing on the best creates exclusion and rewards the performative.
points: Learning is best defined as getting better and making that improvement sticky, not as being the best or getting everything right.
A getting-better mindset takes pressure off perfection and credits improvement, which is what Kane credits for his growth from good player to best in the world.
Teachers should design good struggle that is difficult enough to require effort but not so difficult that students conclude they cannot improve.
Schools should celebrate who has improved and how in newsletters, prize days and noticeboards, since celebrating the best creates exclusivity.
quotes: No matter what I achieve, how many goals I score, winning the Ballon 'd’Or, it’s always about getting better.
You’ll notice he doesn’t say ‘Being the best.’ He says ‘Getting better.
Quite literally, we are in the business of helping people get better, little by little. That’s it.
Getting better means knowing more knowledge about something than we did previously but not necessarily knowing everything.
A focus on getting better takes the pressure off not being perfect; it allows us to gain credit for our improvement without having to be the best.
experiences which are difficult enough to require children and students to struggle well and to learn that they can get better but not so difficult that they learn that they can’t.

Making the ‘best’ the focus of a school’s celebrations creates exclusivity and exclusion for many and can reward the performative; making ‘getting better’ the focus creates inclusivity; it rewards the act of learning and improvement.
